passages.original: divini- tate] descendisse, et hoc modo ostendisset eorum quae naturaliter insunt utrique naturae unius Christi et Dei Filii per commutationem summam redditionem, sub- infert : « Unde, inquiens, et unam voluntatem fatemur Domini Jesu Christi, » quomodo ait : « Quia profecto a divinitate assumpta est natura nostra, non culpa, » id est, non a peccato, propemodum cum magno effatus Athanasio, qui haec contra Apollinarium impium scribit : « Natus est ex muliere, de prima plasmatione hominis formam sibi erigens in ostentione carnis absque carnalibus voluntatibus, et humanis cogita- tionibus in imagine novitatis. Voluntas enim sola divinitatis est, quoniam natura tota divinitatis est.
passages.english: [...] had come down [with the divinity], and had in this way shown the supreme rendering, by exchange, of the things that naturally belong to each nature of the one Christ and Son of God, he adds: "Whence," he says, "we also confess one will of the Lord Jesus Christ," in the way that he says: "Because indeed our nature was assumed by the divinity, not [our] guilt," that is, not [our nature] as subject to sin, speaking almost in agreement with the great Athanasius, who writes these things against the impious Apollinarius: "He was born of a woman, raising up for himself the form of man from the first fashioning, in the display of flesh without carnal wills, and without human thoughts, in the image of newness. For the will is of the divinity alone, since the whole nature is of the divinity."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence: the context before ends with an editorial bracket "[Leg." ("read"), so "divinitate]" closes an editor's proposed reading, apparently "humanitas de coelo cum divinitate" ("the humanity [came down] from heaven with the divinity"). "ostentione" is taken as "ostentatione" (display). "non a peccato" is literally "not from/by sin". The sense of "summam redditionem" ("supreme rendering/return") is uncertain; it may refer to the communication of properties. The last sentence of the Athanasius quotation is obscure and may be corrupt. It reads literally "the whole nature is of the divinity"; the sense may be that the whole nature [that wills] is the divinity's.
